\chapter{Synthesis --- Saying Something About Your Own Life}
\label{ch:spanish-synthesis-describing}
\hlchaptermodality{152}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can describe things around me with the nouns and colours I hold, choosing un rather than el.}

Fourteen chapters of nouns and colours, combined for the first time - and the article that makes it possible.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Practice]{Synthesis — saying something about your own life}

\label{lesson:ES-C40-sintesis-describir}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new in this chapter. Say the words for \emph{dog} and for \emph{black}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Something has been accumulating quietly for fourteen chapters and has never once been put to work.

You have six colours. Parents and brothers and sisters. A head and a hand. Water, wine and bread. The seasons, the months, the hours. Hot weather and cold. Numbers to twenty. A dog and a cat.

That is not a vocabulary list any more. It is \textbf{enough to describe the room you are sitting in}, and this chapter is the first that asks you to.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the word that made this possible}]
Notice which article you need here, because it is not the one you have used most.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{el perro} — \emph{the} dog. A particular one. The one we were talking about. \textbf{un perro} — \emph{a} dog. Any dog. One you are mentioning for the first time.
\end{quote}

Describing your own life means introducing things your listener does not know about yet — and that is exactly the job \textbf{un} does. Almost every sentence below needs it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\begin{quote}
— ¿\textbf{Tienes un perro}? — Sí, \textbf{tengo un perro negro}. ¿Y tú? — \textbf{Tengo un gato blanco.}
\end{quote}

Every word in those three lines is one you built yourself, across fourteen chapters that never asked you to combine them. Nothing here is new. What is new is that it is a \textbf{conversation} rather than a list.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the exchange above, both parts
  \item it again about a real animal you know, with a real colour
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} Until you are describing rather than translating.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which article introduces something your listener does not yet know about? (\textbf{Un}.) And which points at something you have both already mentioned? (\textbf{El}.) Say one true sentence about an animal, with its colour.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(review)]{Review — the same question, asked of eleven words}

\label{lesson:ES-C40-repaso-palabras-con-historia}



\begin{quote}
The two days of the weekend. (\emph{Sábado, domingo}.) The four seasons. (\emph{Primavera, verano, otoño, invierno}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now say when something happens.

The hour: \emph{Son las dos.} Add the minutes: \emph{Son las dos y} \textbf{veinte}. The two hinges of the day: \emph{el mediodía}, \emph{la medianoche}. And the weather, which needs no subject at all — \emph{llueve}.

The months, in order, from \emph{enero} to \emph{diciembre}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
Ask one question of all of them — \emph{where did you come from?} — and no two give the same answer.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{\textbf{la hora}} came through from Latin nearly untouched.
  \item \emph{\textbf{veinte}} came through worn thin, but in one piece.
  \item \emph{\textbf{sábado}} and \emph{\textbf{domingo}} were \textbf{overwritten}: the other five days are named after planets, and a religion renamed these two.
  \item \emph{\textbf{azul}} was \textbf{borrowed}, from Arabic, and then beat the inherited word.
  \item \emph{\textbf{verde}} was a verb before it was a colour — \textquotedblleft{}to flourish.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{\textbf{amarillo}} meant \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}a little bitter.\textquotedblright{}} It has no ancestor that meant yellow at all.
  \item \emph{\textbf{rojo}} is a \textbf{cousin} of French \emph{rouge}, not a copy of it.
\end{itemize}

Inherited, worn, overwritten, borrowed, repurposed, drifted, related. Every new word you meet from here on has one of those behind it, and asking which is how a vocabulary stops being a list.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sábado}, \emph{domingo} — then \emph{lunes}, and hear the planet come back
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name the season after \emph{el verano}. (\emph{El otoño}.) The month after \emph{noviembre}. (\emph{Diciembre}.) And which of your colour words was borrowed rather than inherited? (\emph{\textbf{Azul}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(review)]{Review — one Saturday, from morning to midnight}

\label{lesson:ES-C40-repaso-un-sabado-de-octubre}



\begin{quote}
The first day of the weekend. (\emph{El sábado}.) The month before \emph{noviembre}. (\emph{Octubre}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Every piece below has been a separate chapter. Here they are as one day.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Es \textbf{sábado}. Es \textbf{octubre}, y es \textbf{otoño}.} \emph{Son las nueve y \textbf{veinte}. \textbf{Llueve}.} \emph{Al \textbf{mediodía} el cielo está \textbf{amarillo}.} \emph{A \textbf{medianoche}, todavía \textbf{llueve}.}
\end{quote}

Read it again and count what it took: a day name, a month, a season, an hour, the minutes, a weather verb with nothing in front of it, two halves of the day, and a colour. Nine chapters, four lines.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
One thing in that story is quietly wrong, and it has been wrong for two thousand years.

\emph{\textbf{Octubre}} carries \emph{ocho} inside it. Eight. And it is the \textbf{tenth} month.

The Roman year opened in March, so the counting started there: \emph{septiembre} seventh, \emph{octubre} eighth, \emph{noviembre} ninth, \emph{diciembre} tenth. Then the year was moved to January, everything slid by two, and nobody renamed anything.

So four of your months are still counting from a new year that stopped happening — which is why you can read them without being told what they mean.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the four lines of the story, straight through, without stopping
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What day was it? (\emph{\textbf{Sábado}}.) What colour was the sky at noon? (\emph{\textbf{Amarillo}}.) And what number is hiding in \emph{diciembre}? (\emph{\textbf{Diez}} — ten, in the tenth month's old position.)
\end{tcolorbox}
